title: Create in me a clean heart (Psalm 51)
hookLine: David's prayer after his great wrong: a broken heart you won't despise

cards: The prophet Nathan walks into the palace with a story about two men in one town. One rich, with flocks and herds.
One poor, with a single little ewe lamb he raised with his own children, that ate from his plate and slept in his arms.
A guest arrives, and instead of taking from his own flocks, the rich man takes the poor man's lamb and serves it for dinner. King David is furious. That man deserves to die, he says.
And Nathan answers with four words: "Thou art the man." David has taken Bathsheba, another man's wife, and arranged for her husband Uriah to die in battle.

teach.b: Psalm fifty-one begins, in the King James Bible: "Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness." No excuses. He asks to be washed, thoroughly, and cleansed.
Then verse ten: "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." Create. In Hebrew it's bara, the same verb as the first line of the Bible, in the beginning God created.
In its usual form, the Bible uses it only with God as the one doing it. So David isn't asking for a stain remover.
He's asking God to do for his heart what God did for the world: make something new where there was only chaos. Sacrifices and offerings, he says, aren't what God is after.
"The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise." Contrite means crushed, ground down.
The thing you'd expect God to turn away from, the wreckage, is the one thing he won't refuse.

teach.h: CREATE IN ME A CLEAN HEART, O GOD.
teach.b: Readers differ on whether the headings were part of the psalms from the start; tradition hears this one as David's own. In Latin it's called the Miserere, from its first word.
Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans pray it in Lent and on Ash Wednesday, and the daily prayer of some churches opens each morning with its verse fifteen: O Lord, open thou my lips.

how: Psalm 51 is a prayer of repentance across the churches: Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans pray it in Lent and on Ash Wednesday, and some Christians pray verse 10 before confession or at the start of the day.

o: to forgive, to let a debt go unpaid
to wash clean, the way you scrub a stain
to create, the verb of in the beginning

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: told the story of the one lamb
a broken and a contrite heart

s: Psalm 51 asks God only to wash David clean
it asks to be washed, and then asks God to create a clean heart: something new, not just scrubbed.
Psalm 51 is called the Miserere, from its first Latin word
the Latin begins miserere mei, Deus: have mercy on me, O God.
in this psalm, God refuses a broken heart
"a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."

games.q: you're King David. the prophet has just told you about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb, and you're furious. then he says: thou art the man. what do you do?
o: say, I have sinned against the LORD.
explain why your case was different.
games.why: David says, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13). no defense. Psalm 51's heading places the psalm right after this moment.

practice: Think of one place where you keep cleaning up the same mess, the same sharp tone, the same apology, and instead of scrubbing at it again, picture one concrete scene of a new start: what you'd say, what you'd do first.
If you pray, say verse ten slowly: create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me. If you don't, simply hold the picture.

wordCard.voice: Bara. Hebrew for create, the same verb as in the beginning God created: what David asks for his own heart, not scrubbed clean, but made new.

orig.note: Hebrew: a clean heart. tahor is the word for clean, pure, fit to come near God.

carryVoice: Your line: a clean heart. Asked for with no excuses at all. That's four hundred twenty-four.
